hints: Look carefully at the shape of the curve: it rises steeply between R and S, but goes flat and horizontal between S and T. What does a flat line tell you about adding more substrate?

Remember the limiting factor rule: if adding more substrate increases the rate, substrate is limiting. If adding more substrate does nothing, the active sites are all full so enzyme concentration is limiting.
walkthrough:
**Read the shape of the graph**

Think of this like seats on a bus. Between R and S the curve is going up, so every extra bit of substrate gives a faster rate. Between S and T the curve is flat, so extra substrate makes no difference at all.

**Apply the limiting factor idea**

When the rate is rising, substrate is in short supply and is limiting the rate. There are plenty of free active sites waiting. When the rate plateaus, all active sites are occupied and saturated, so adding substrate cannot help.

**Pick the correct region**

The plateau from S to T means the enzymes are working as fast as they can at Vmax. Here the fixed number of enzyme molecules is what limits any further increase. That matches statement C.

options.A: Between R and S the rate is still rising, so there are still free active sites. Substrate, not enzyme, is limiting here.
options.B: Product concentration does not limit the initial rate in this graph. The rise between R and S is controlled by substrate availability.
options.C: Between S and T the graph plateaus despite more substrate, showing all active sites are saturated. The constant number of enzyme molecules now limits the rate.
options.D: Between S and T substrate is in excess, as shown by the flat line. Adding more substrate molecules has no effect, so substrate is not limiting.
